title: The Department of Agriculture announces it would not distribute SNAP benefits for
description_short: The Department of Agriculture announces it would not distribute SNAP benefits for November 2025 due to the ongoing shutdown
description_medium: On October 26, 2025, USDA said Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits would not be distributed for November during the federal shutdown. The program serves more than 40 million people. The department declined to use its contingency reserve, saying it was for emergencies; a budget-policy group estimated the reserve could cover about 60% of one month. Some states said they could not replace the federal funds.
description_long: The U.S. Department of Agriculture said on October 26, 2025, that Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits would not be distributed beginning in November because of the federal shutdown. SNAP assists more than 40 million people, roughly one in eight Americans. The department said its contingency reserve was for “true emergencies,” while the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities estimated that the reserve could cover about 60% of one month’s benefits. House Democrats urged Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins to release that money and transfer other available funds to cover the program; several states said they lacked enough resources to make up any shortfall. The BBC reported that the federal government would not reimburse states that used their own funds. The story records the department’s announced position and the dispute over whether emergency reserves could bridge the shutdown. It does not establish that every state or household ultimately went without benefits for the full month. The immediate event was a federal funding decision with potential consequences for food assistance, not a final account of the interruption’s duration or state-by-state effects.
organization_tags: Center on Budget and Policy Priorities

title: Trump threatens ‘a big hit’ if Tehran does not make deal soon
description_short: Trump threatens ‘a big hit’ if Tehran does not make deal soon
description_medium: On May 19, 2026, Trump threatened new attacks on Iran if it did not make concessions for a deal and said he had been an hour from ordering strikes before calling them off. The Guardian reported that Tehran had sent a proposal through Pakistan during a ceasefire and that Trump threatened a “big hit” within days. Iran rejected U.S. demands as excessive; no new strike had occurred when the article was published.
description_long: On May 19, 2026, Donald Trump threatened a new “big hit” against Iran if Tehran did not make concessions toward a deal. He said he had been an hour from deciding to launch another wave of strikes but had called it off after Iran sent a further peace proposal through Pakistan, which was mediating. The planned attacks would have broken a ceasefire that had been in place since early April. Trump said a new attack could come within days; Iranian officials called U.S. demands excessive and warned that Iran would open new fronts if attacked. The Guardian described the conflict as deadlocked: Washington and Tehran had held one unsuccessful round of talks, while Iran continued to restrict shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and the United States maintained a naval blockade of Iranian ports. The article reports a threat and a decision to defer a strike, not a new attack. It places the warning in the context of stalled negotiations and competing ceasefire proposals, while noting that allies were reluctant to see hostilities resume. The source does not say that a final agreement had been reached.
subcategory: Threat of renewed military strikes during Iran negotiations

title: Norway Moves Toward Formal FIFA Ethics Complaint Over Trump-Balogun Intervention
description_short: Norway Moves Toward Formal FIFA Ethics Complaint Over Trump-Balogun Intervention
description_medium: The supplied correction context identifies a different event from the current headline: Norway’s football association supported an ethics complaint concerning FIFA president Gianni Infantino after FIFA’s Peace Prize for Donald Trump, alleging a breach of political neutrality. The linked AP page returned HTTP 403, so the complaint’s exact wording and chronology could not be confirmed. The Balogun-ban account is not supported by that source.
subcategory: FIFA ethics complaint and political neutrality

preserved_fields.title: Norway Moves Toward Formal FIFA Ethics Complaint Over Trump-Balogun Intervention
preserved_fields.description_short: Norway Moves Toward Formal FIFA Ethics Complaint Over Trump-Balogun Intervention
preserved_fields.description_medium: The Norwegian Football Association, led by president Lise Klaveness, moved to formally file a complaint with FIFA's ethics investigators over President Trump's documented role in clearing Folarin Balogun from his mandatory one-game ban. Klaveness stated publicly: "We all know that this verdict was influenced from external forces and did not have the proper process." The complaint follows Belgium's 4-1 elimination of the US — the match at the center of the scandal — and positions Norway as the leading national federation challenging FIFA's capitulation to American presidential pressure.

notes: The linked AP page returned HTTP 403. The supplied correction context says AP reported that Norway filed a letter supporting an ethics complaint against FIFA president Gianni Infantino after the FIFA Peace Prize, alleging political-neutrality violations. It says a separate report—not this AP story—covered Trump’s call and FIFA’s decision about Folarin Balogun. The current title and synopsis conflate these events and date them incorrectly. Proposed correction: retitle around Norway’s ethics-complaint letter concerning Infantino and FIFA’s Peace Prize; do not attribute the separate Balogun decision to this AP story.
proposed_correction: Norway Supports FIFA Ethics Complaint Concerning Infantino and the FIFA Peace Prize

title: Trump Fires Bondi for Insufficient Weaponization — Epstein Files Buried Under New AG
